newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY UNION-UNHERALDED ACT STUN SUPER 12 HEAVYWEIGHTS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-UNHERALDED ACT STUN SUPER 12 HEAVYWEIGHTS.

text.p: Australian Capital Territory (ACT), the surprise package of southern hemisphere rugby union this season, face the ultimate test of their credentials as Super 12 leaders on Saturday when they visit champions Auckland.
But whatever the outcome at Eden Park, the unheralded Brumbies have already done enough to confound the odds by topping the Super 12 standings at the season's half-way stage.
In the process, the Canberra-based team have overshadowed New South Wales and Queensland, the traditional heavyweights of Australian rugby.
And they have done so with a team built largely from scratch over the past two years following rugby union's switch to open professionalism.
Furthermore, they have relied heavily on players discarded by New South Wales and Queensland. Given first choice of the available talent, they moved quickly.
Only when the dust had settled did ACT coach Rod Macqueen mould together a side from what remained -- a collection of untested locals, aging former internationals and reserves.

"As a coach I gained a lot of satisfaction from putting together a winning team from that situation. But there is a long way to go this season and a lot of rugby still to be played," Macqueen said in an interview.
"I think it is a mistake to say that our players are discards, but it is true to say a majority of the players who came to us were not playing at the time for New South Wales or Queensland.
"There are only 30 places available in a Super 12 squad and there was obviously quite a lot of talent left over after they had finished recruiting.
"But the players here have shown they are capable of performing at provincial level. It is a very positive development for Australian rugby," Macqueen said.
What they lack in tradition and money, ACT have compensated for with an inventive style of rugby that has seen them score 223 points, the highest tally in the competition.
ACT top the Super 12 standings with 21 points, although their nearest rivals Natal, Auckland and Gauteng Lions, formerly Transvaal, have a game in hand.
But with the top four teams qualifying for the semifinals, Macqueen appears poised to pull off a major upset in the second year of his two-year contract.

With the advent of professionalism two years ago, the Australian Rugby Union (ARU), the sport's national ruling body, successfully lobbied for ACT's introduction into Super 12, involving sides from Australia, South Africa and New Zealand.
Previously, the Brumbies -- named after the wild horses that roam the highlands near the national capital-- had to be satisfied with occasional matches against overseas touring sides.
But in formulating a professional structure domestically, ARU chiefs created a funding arrangement that greatly favoured New South Wales and Queensland.
In effect, teams were rewarded according to the number of test players already on their books, a decision that benefitted the existing powers.
At the time only two Brumbies -- scrum-half George Gregan and winger Joe Roff -- were Wallaby internationals, leaving ACT with A$1.6 million (US$1.2 million) less to spend on wages.
Although worse off financially, Macqueen at least had enough money to secure the services of highly-rated prop Patricio Noriega of Argentina to strengthen the front row.
In another key acquisition, former Wallaby fly-half David Knox arrived from New South Wales, where he faced an uncertain future, in a move that has revitalised his career.
"Players were happy to come to Canberra rather than warming the reserves bench or waiting for another player to be injured elsewhere," Macqueen said.
Last weekend, the Brumbies overwhelmed South Africa's Free State 50-23 at Bruce Stadium, stretching an unbeaten record at home to nine matches since the competition started last year.
"Our last performance was the closest we have come to putting together 80 minutes of football the way we want to play the game," Macqueen said.
